blocks.text: Imagine you asked a friend to read a document out loud to you once, and then you never checked back in. If that document changes later, you would have no idea, you would just keep repeating stale information from memory.

A client talking to an MCP server has exactly this problem with resources. It reads a file, a database row, a config value, once, and then has to decide, somehow, whether that reading is still trustworthy.
This lesson is about the mechanisms MCP gives a client to answer that question, from simple polling to real notifications, and the tradeoffs between them.
1. Why a Client Needs to Know About Change
Resources are not frozen snapshots. A log file grows, a config value gets edited, a database row updates as business events happen.
If a client reads a resource once and holds onto that content forever, it will eventually show a user something wrong, sometimes embarrassingly wrong.
Think of a coding assistant reading a source file, then suggesting an edit based on a version of that file that was already replaced five minutes ago.
So MCP needs some way for a server to say, this thing you read earlier is not the same anymore, go take another look.
2. Two Very Different Kinds of Change

blocks.alt: A single resource updating is one kind of change and the whole list changing is another

blocks.text: There are really two separate questions a client might care about, and MCP treats them as two separate notifications.
The first question is, has the content of this one specific resource I already know about changed underneath me.
The second question is, has the overall set of resources this server offers changed, meaning something new appeared or something old disappeared.
Confusing these two would be like mixing up a chapter being edited with a whole book being removed from the shelf, they call for different responses.
3. The resources/updated Notification

blocks.alt: A server sends an updated notification when one resource changes

blocks.text: When the content behind one particular resource uri changes, and a client has expressed interest in that uri, the server can send a resources/updated notification.
This notification names exactly one uri. It does not carry the new content itself, it is just a signal, go read this again.
Notice there is no id field, this is a notification, not a request, so the server never expects a reply to it.
4. What a Client Does After resources/updated
Receiving the notification is only step one. The client still has to actually go fetch the fresh content before anything useful happens.
In practice this means calling resources/read again with that same uri, and replacing whatever stale copy it was holding onto.

blocks.title: Notifications describe, they do not deliver
blocks.content: A resources/updated message never carries the new content inline. It only ever points at a uri, the client must always follow up with its own resources/read call.

blocks.text: 5. The resources/list_changed Notification

blocks.alt: A server sends a list changed notification when the whole set changes

blocks.text: The second notification, resources/list_changed, is about the shape of the whole collection, not the content of any single item.
A server sends this when a resource is added, removed, or renamed, anything that means the previous resources/list result is now out of date.
This message carries no parameters at all. It does not say which resource changed, only that the client should call resources/list again to see the current picture.
6. Comparing the Two Notifications
Side by side, these two notifications answer different sized questions, and trigger different follow up calls.

blocks.text: 7. Subscribing to a Specific Resource

blocks.alt: A client subscribes to one resource so the server tracks it for changes

blocks.text: A server usually will not send resources/updated for every resource it holds, that could be an overwhelming flood of noise for things nobody is even looking at.
Instead, MCP defines an optional resources/subscribe request, letting a client say, specifically, I care about this one uri, please tell me if it changes.
Only servers that advertise a subscribe capability during initialization support this request, it is entirely optional for a server to implement.
8. Unsubscribing When Interest Ends
A client that no longer cares about a resource, say the user closed the file it was watching, should clean up with resources/unsubscribe.
This matters more than it might first seem. A server tracking subscriptions for hundreds of long lived clients needs some way to stop watching things nobody wants anymore.
9. A Concrete Subscribe, Change, Notify Flow

blocks.alt: A subscribe call is followed by a change and then a notify

blocks.text: Here is the full sequence end to end, from the moment a client decides it cares about a resource to the moment it sees fresh content.
Notice that the server itself has to be watching the underlying resource somehow, subscribing does not create that watching for free, the server still has to implement it.
10. Simple Approach One, Re Reading and Comparing Content

blocks.alt: Re reading and comparing content is compared against using a version tag

blocks.text: Not every client, and not every server, wants to deal with subscriptions at all. A much simpler approach is to just re read a resource periodically and compare it to the last copy you had.
This needs no special server support beyond ordinary resources/read, it works against any MCP server, subscribe capable or not.
The obvious downside is cost, comparing full content on every check can be wasteful for large resources, and it still needs some external timer deciding when to check.
11. Simple Approach Two, a Version Tag
A cheaper variant is for the server to expose a small version marker alongside a resource, a hash, a timestamp, a revision number, anything short.
A client can then compare just that small marker instead of the entire content, only pulling the full body when the marker actually differs.
MCP does not mandate a specific versioning field, so this is a convention a server author chooses, a modification timestamp and a content hash are both common choices.
12. Polling Versus Subscription, the Core Tradeoff

blocks.alt: Polling is compared against subscription as the core tradeoff

blocks.text: Polling means the client decides when to check, on some timer, whether anything changed, whether by re reading content or by comparing a version tag.
Subscription means the server decides when to speak up, pushing a notification only at the moment something actually changes.
Polling is simple to build and works everywhere, but it either wastes effort checking too often, or misses changes by checking too rarely.
Subscription is more efficient and near instant, but it demands more from the server, real change detection, tracking who is subscribed, and cleanup when clients disconnect.
13. Choosing Between Them in Practice

blocks.content: {"headers":["Situation","Reasonable choice"],"rows":[["Resource rarely changes, staleness is low stakes","Simple polling with a version tag"],["Resource changes often and freshness really matters","Subscribe if the server supports it"],["Server does not support subscribe at all","Fall back to periodic re reading"],["Client only needs the resource once, briefly","Skip both, just read once"]]}

blocks.text: None of these are permanent commitments, a client can start with polling and switch to subscription later if the server adds support for it.
14. What Happens Without Any of This
It is worth being explicit about the failure mode this whole lesson exists to prevent, since it makes the motivation concrete.

items: A client reads a config file once at startup and never checks again, so a later edit silently has zero effect.
A client shows a cached list of resources, so a newly added document never appears in a search.
A client acts on a deleted resource's old content, since nothing ever told it the resource was gone.

blocks.text: Every one of these is avoidable, either with notifications, with polling, or at minimum by being honest with a user that the data might be stale.
15. Notification Capability Declaration
A server that supports subscriptions says so during initialization, inside its resources capability object, so a client knows up front whether subscribe is even worth trying.
If subscribe is missing or false here, a client should not bother sending resources/subscribe, it would just get an error back for an unsupported method.
Worked Example
Suppose a client is watching a build log file that a server exposes as a resource, and wants to keep a terminal view live updated.
First, the client checks the server's advertised capabilities, sees subscribe is true, and sends a subscribe request for that log file's uri.

code.content:
# 1. subscribe once
await client.subscribe_resource(uri="log://build/12938")

# 2. keep a simple in memory cache of the last content
last_seen = None

async def on_resources_updated(uri):
    global last_seen
    result = await client.read_resource(uri=uri)
    new_content = result.contents[0].text
    if new_content != last_seen:
        print("New log lines:")
        print(new_content[len(last_seen or ""):])
        last_seen = new_content

blocks.text: Each time a resources/updated notification arrives for that uri, the handler re reads, diffs against the last seen copy, and prints only the new part.
When the build finishes and the terminal view closes, the client sends resources/unsubscribe so the server can stop tracking it.
Common Mistakes

items: Assuming resources/updated carries the new content, then trying to read it straight off the notification instead of calling resources/read.
Subscribing to a resource and never unsubscribing, leaving a server tracking interest that no longer exists.
Polling as fast as possible out of caution, creating needless load instead of picking a sensible interval.
Treating resources/list_changed as if it named the specific resource that changed, when it carries no uri at all.
Calling resources/subscribe on a server that never advertised the subscribe capability, and being surprised by an error.
Comparing full content byte by byte on every poll when a cheap version tag would have done the same job for less cost.

blocks.text: Practice
Design a small versioning scheme for a server that exposes a shopping cart as a resource, one that changes every time an item is added or removed.
Decide what your version tag looks like, whether you would use subscribe or polling, and sketch the one notification or request you would send when the cart changes.
Key Takeaway

A resource's content can drift away from what a client last saw, so MCP gives servers two focused notifications, resources/updated for one specific uri and resources/list_changed for the whole collection.

Subscribe and unsubscribe let a client opt into just the resources it cares about, while simple re reading or version tag comparisons remain a perfectly valid fallback, trading a little efficiency for far less complexity.
